\title{
Batch and match: black-box variational inference with a score-based divergence
}

\author{
Diana Cai ${ }^{1}$ Chirag Modi ${ }^{12}$ Loucas Pillaud-Vivien ${ }^{13}$ Charles C. Margossian ${ }^{1}$ Robert M. Gower ${ }^{1}$ David M. Blei ${ }^{4}$ Lawrence K. Saul ${ }^{1}$

\begin{abstract}
Most leading implementations of black-box variational inference (BBVI) are based on optimizing a stochastic evidence lower bound (ELBO). But such approaches to BBVI often converge slowly due to the high variance of their gradient estimates and their sensitivity to hyperparameters. In this work, we propose batch and match (BaM), an alternative approach to BBVI based on a scorebased divergence. Notably, this score-based divergence can be optimized by a closed-form proximal update for Gaussian variational families with full covariance matrices. We analyze the convergence of BaM when the target distribution is Gaussian, and we prove that in the limit of infinite batch size the variational parameter updates converge exponentially quickly to the target mean and covariance. We also evaluate the performance of BaM on Gaussian and non-Gaussian target distributions that arise from posterior inference in hierarchical and deep generative models. In these experiments, we find that BaM typically converges in fewer (and sometimes significantly fewer) gradient evaluations than leading implementations of BBVI based on ELBO maximization.
\end{abstract}

\subsection*{2.2. The score-based divergence}

We now introduce the score-based divergence, which will be the basis for a BBVI objective. Here we focus on a Gaussian variational family, i.e.,
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\left\{\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma): \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{D}, \Sigma \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^{D}\right\}
\]
but we generalize the score-based divergence to nonGaussian distributions in Appendix A.

The score-based divergence between densities $q \in \mathcal{Q}$ and $p$ on $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ is defined as
\[
\mathscr{D}(q ; p):=\int\left\|\nabla_{z} \log \left(\frac{q(z)}{p(z)}\right)\right\|_{\operatorname{Cov}(q)}^{2} q(z) d z
\]
where $\operatorname{Cov}(q) \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^{D}$ is the covariance matrix of the variational density $q$.
Importantly, the score-based divergence can be evaluated when $p$ is only known up to a normalization constant, as it only depends on the target density through the score $\nabla \log p$. Thus, not only can this divergence be used as a VI objective, but it can also be used for goodness-of-fit evaluations, unlike the KL divergence.

The divergence in eq. (2) is well-defined under mild conditions on $p$ and $q$ (see Appendix A), and it enjoys two important properties:

Property 1 (Non-negativity \& equality): $\mathscr{D}(q ; p) \geq 0$ with $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)=0$ iff $p=q$.
Property 2 (Affine invariance): Let $h: \mathbb{R}^{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{D}$ be an affine transformation, and consider the induced densities $\tilde{q}(h(z))=q(z)|\mathcal{J}(z)|^{-1}$ and $\tilde{p}(h(z))=$ $p(z)|\mathcal{J}(z)|^{-1}$, where $\mathcal{J}$ is the determinant of the Jacobian of $h$. Then $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)=\mathscr{D}(\tilde{q} ; \tilde{p})$.

We note that these properties are also satisfied by the KL divergence (Qiao \& Minematsu, 2010). The first property shows that $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)$ is a proper divergence measuring the agreement between $p$ and $q$. The second property states that the score-based divergence $\mathscr{D}(q, p)$ is invariant under affine transformations; this property is desirable to maintain a consistent measure of similarity under coordinate transformations of the input. This property depends crucially on the weighted vector norm, mediated by $\operatorname{Cov}(q)$, in the divergence of eq. (2).
There are several related divergences in the research literature. A generalization of the score-based divergence is the weighted Fisher divergence (Barp et al., 2019), given by $\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\|\nabla \log (q / p)\|_{M}^{2}\right]$, where $M \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$; the score-based divergence is recovered by the choice $M=\operatorname{Cov}(q)$. A special case of the score-based divergence is the Fisher divergence (Hyvärinen, 2005) given by $\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\|\nabla \log (q / p)\|_{I}^{2}\right]$, but this divergence is not affine invariant. (See the proof of Theorem A. 4 for further discussion.)

\section*{3. Score-based Gaussian variational inference}

The score-based divergence has many favorable properties for VI. We now show that this divergence can also be efficiently optimized by an iterative black-box algorithm.

\subsection*{3.1. Algorithm}

Our goal is to find some Gaussian distribution $q^{*} \in \mathcal{Q}$ that minimizes $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)$. Without additional assumptions on the target $p$, the score-based divergence $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)$ is not analytically tractable. So instead we consider a Monte Carlo estimate of $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)$ : given samples $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{B} \sim q$, we construct the approximation
\[
\mathscr{D}(q ; p) \approx \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B}\left\|\nabla_{z} \log \left(\frac{q\left(z_{b}\right)}{p\left(z_{b}\right)}\right)\right\|_{\operatorname{Cov}(q)}^{2}
\]

This estimator is unbiased, but it does not lend itself to optimization: we cannot simultaneously sample from $q$ while also optimizing over the family $\mathcal{Q}$ to which it belongs. There is a generic solution to the above problem: the so-called "reparameterization trick" (e.g., Kucukelbir et al. (2017)) decouples the sampling distribution and optimization variable. But this approach leads to a gradient-based algorithm that does not fully capitalize on the structure of the Gaussian variational family.
In this paper we take a different approach, one that does capitalize on this structure. Specifically, we take an iterative approach whose goal is to produce a sequence of distributions $\left\{q_{t}\right\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$ that converges to $q^{*}$. At a high level, the approach alternates between two steps-one that constructs a biased estimate of $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)$, and another that updates $q$ based on this biased estimate, but not too aggressively (so as to minimize the effect of the bias). Specifically, at the $t^{\text {th }}$ iteration, we first estimate $\mathscr{D}(q ; p)$ with samples from $q_{t}$ : i.e., given $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{B} \sim q_{t}$, we compute
\[
\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q_{t}}(q ; p):=\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B}\left\|\nabla_{z} \log \left(\frac{q\left(z_{b}\right)}{p\left(z_{b}\right)}\right)\right\|_{\operatorname{Cov}(q)}^{2}
\]

We call eq. (4) the batch step because it estimates $\mathscr{D}(q, p)$ from the batch of samples $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{B} \sim q_{t}$.
The batch step of the algorithm relies on stochastic sampling, but it alternates with a deterministic step that updates $q$ by minimizing the empirical score-based divergence $\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q_{t}}(q ; p)$ in eq. (4). Importantly, this minimization is subject to a regularizer: we penalize large differences between $q_{t}$ and $q_{t+1}$ by their KL divergence. Intuitively, when $q$ remains close to $q_{t}$, then $\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q_{t}}(q ; p)$ in eq. (4) remains a good approximation to the unbiased estimate $\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q}(q ; p)$ in eq. (3). With this in mind, we compute $q_{t+1}$ by minimizing the regularized objective function
\[
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{BaM}}(q):=\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q_{t}}(q ; p)+\frac{2}{\lambda_{t}} \mathrm{KL}\left(q_{t} ; q\right)
\]
where $q \in \mathcal{Q}$ and $\lambda_{t}>0$ is the inverse regularization parameter. When $\lambda_{t}$ is small, the regularizer is large, encouraging the next iterate $q_{t+1}$ to remain close to $q_{t}$; thus $\lambda_{t}$ can also be viewed as a learning rate.

The objective function in eq. (5) has the important property that its global minimum can be computed analytically in closed form. In particular, we can optimize eq. (5) without recourse to gradient-based methods that are derived from a linearization around $q_{t}$. We refer to the minimization of $\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{BaM}}(q)$ in eq. (5) as the match step because the updated distribution $q_{t+1}$ always matches the scores at $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{B}$ better than the current one $q_{t}$.
Combining these two steps, we arrive at the batch and match (BaM) algorithm for BBVI with a score-based divergence. The intuition behind this iterative approach will be formally justified in Section 3.2 by a proof of convergence. We now discuss each step of the algorithm in greater detail.

Batch Step. This step begins by sampling $z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots, z_{B} \sim$ $q_{t}$ and computing the scores $g_{b}=\nabla \log p\left(z_{b}\right)$ at each sample. It then calculates the means and covariances (over the batch) of these quantities; we denote these statistics by
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\bar{z}=\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} z_{b}, & C=\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B}\left(z_{b}-\bar{z}\right)\left(z_{b}-\bar{z}\right)^{\top} \\
\bar{g}=\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} g_{b}, & \Gamma=\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B}\left(g_{b}-\bar{g}\right)\left(g_{b}-\bar{g}\right)^{\top}
\end{array}
\]
where $\bar{z}, \bar{g} \in \mathbb{R}^{D}$ are the means, respectively, of the samples and the scores, and $C, \Gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ are their covariances. In Appendix C, we show that the empirical score-based divergence $\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q_{t}}(q ; p)$ in eq. (4) can be written in terms of these statistics as
$\widehat{\mathscr{D}}_{q_{t}}(q ; p)=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma \Sigma)+\operatorname{tr}\left(C \Sigma^{-1}\right)+\|\mu-\bar{z}-\Sigma \bar{g}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}+$ const.,
where for clarity we have suppressed additive constants that do not depend on the mean $\mu$ or covariance $\Sigma$ of $q$. This calculation completes the batch step of BaM.
Match Step. The match step of BaM updates the variational approximation $q$ by setting
\[
q_{t+1}=\arg \min _{q \in \mathcal{Q}} \mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{BaM}}(q)
\]
where $\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{BaM}}(q)$ is given by eq. (5). This optimization can be solved in closed form; that is, we can analytically calculate the variational mean $\mu_{t+1}$ and covariance $\Sigma_{t+1}$ that minimize $\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{BaM}}(q)$.
The details of this calculation are given in Appendix C. There we show that the updated covariance $\Sigma_{t+1}$ satisfies a quadratic matrix equation,
\[
\Sigma_{t+1} U \Sigma_{t+1}+\Sigma_{t+1}=V
\]
where the matrices $U$ and $V$ in this expression are positive semidefinite and determined by statistics from the batch step

More intuition for BaM can be obtained by examining certain limiting cases of the batch size and learning rate. When $\lambda_{t} \rightarrow 0$, the updates have no effect, with $\Sigma_{t+1}=\Sigma_{t}$ and $\mu_{t+1}=\mu_{t}$. BaM incorporates many ideas from previous work. Like the stochastic proximal point (SPP) method (Asi \& Duchi, 2019; Davis \& Drusvyatskiy, 2019), it minimizes a Monte Carlo estimate of a divergence subject to a regularization term. In proximal point methods, the updates are always regularized by squared Euclidean distance, but the KL divergence has been used elsewhere as a regularizer-for example, in the EM algorithm (Tseng, 2004; Chrétien \& Hero, 2000) and for approximate Bayesian inference (Theis \& Hoffman, 2015; Khan et al., 2015; 2016; Dai et al., 2016). KL-based regularizers are also a hallmark of mirror descent methods (Nemirovskii \& Yudin, 1983), but in these methods the objective function is linearized-a poor approximation for objective functions with high curvature. Notably, BaM does not introduce any linearizations because its optimizations in eq. (8) can be solved in closed form.

\section*{4. Related work}

BaM builds on intuitions from earlier work on Gaussian score matching (GSM) (Modi et al., 2023). GSM is an iterative algorithm for BBVI that updates a full-covariance Gaussian by analytically solving a system of nonlinear equations. As previously discussed, BaM recovers GSM as a special limiting case. A limitation of GSM is that it aims to match the scores exactly; thus, if the target is not exactly Gaussian, the updates for GSM attempt to solve an infeasible problem, In addition, the batch updates for GSM perform an ad hoc averaging that is not guaranteed to match any scores exactly, even when it is possible to do so. BaM overcomes these limitations by optimizing a proper score-based divergence on each batch of samples. Empirically, with BaM, we observe that larger batch sizes lead to more stable convergence. The score-based divergence behind BaM also lends itself to analysis, and we can provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of BaM for Gaussian targets.

Proximal point methods have been studied in several papers in the context of variational inference; typically the objective is a stochastic estimate of the ELBO with a (forward)

KL regularization term. For example, Theis \& Hoffman (2015) optimize this objective using alternating coordinate ascent. In other work, Khan et al. $(2015 ; 2016)$ propose a splitting method for this objective, and by linearizing the difficult terms, they obtain a closed-form solution when the variational family is Gaussian and additional knowledge is given about the structure of the target. By contrast, BaM does not resort to linearization in order to obtain an analytical solution, nor does it require additional assumptions on the structure of the target.

Proximal algorithms have also been developed for Gaussian variational families based on the Wasserstein metric. Lambert et al. (2022) consider a KL objective with the Wasserstein metric as a regularizer; in this case, the proximal step is not solvable in closed form. On the other hand, Diao et al. (2023) consider a proximal-gradient method, and show that the proximal step admits a closed-form solution.
Several works consider score matching with a Fisher divergence in the context of VI. For instance, Yu \& Zhang (2023) propose a score-matching approach for semi-implicit variational families based on stochastic gradient optimization of the Fisher divergence. Zhang et al. (2018) use the Fisher divergence with an energy-based model as the variational family. BaM differs from these approaches by working with a Gaussian variational family and an affine-invariant score-based divergence.
Finally, we note that the idea of score matching (Hyvärinen, 2005) with a (weighted) Fisher divergence appears in many contexts beyond VI (Song \& Ermon, 2019; Barp et al., 2019). One such context is generative modeling: here, given a set of training examples, the goal is to approximate an unknown data distribution $p$ by a parameterized model $p_{\theta}$ with an intractable normalization constant. Note that in this setting one can evaluate $\nabla \log p_{\theta}$ but not $\nabla \log p$. This setting is quite different from the setting of VI in this paper where we do not have samples from $p$, where we can evaluate $\nabla \log p$, and where the approximating distribution $q$ has the much simpler and more tractable form of a multivariate Gaussian.

\section*{5. Experiments}

We evaluate BaM against two other BBVI methods for Gaussian variational families with full covariance matrices. The first of these is automatic differentiation VI (ADVI) (Kucukelbir et al., 2017), which is based on ELBO maximization, and the second is GSM (Modi et al., 2023), as described in the previous section. We implement all algorithms using JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018), ${ }^{1}$ which supports efficient automatic differentiation both on CPU and GPU. We provide pseudocode for these methods in Appendix E.1.

\subsection*{5.1. Synthetically-constructed target distributions}

We first validate BaM in two settings where we know the true target distribution $p$. In the first setting, we construct Gaussian targets with increasing number of dimensions. In the second setting, we study BaM for distributions with increasing (but controlled) amounts of non-Gaussianity. As evaluation metrics, we use empirical estimates of the KL divergence in both the forward direction, $\operatorname{KL}(p ; q)$, and the reverse direction, $\operatorname{KL}(q ; p)$.

Gaussian targets with increasing dimensions. We construct Gaussian targets of increasing dimension with $D=$ $4,16,64,256$. In Figure 5.1, we compare BaM, ADVI, and GSM on each of these target distributions, plotting the forward KL divergence against the number of gradient evaluations; here we also consider two modified ADVI methods, where instead of the ELBO loss, we use the score-based divergence (labeled as "Score") and the Fisher divergence (labeled as "Fisher"). Results for the reverse KL divergence and other parameter settings are provided in Appendix E.3. In all of these experiments, we use a constant learning rate $\lambda_{t}=B D$ for BaM . Overall, we find that BaM converges orders of magnitude faster than ADVI. While GSM is competitive with BAM in some experiments, BaM converges more quickly with increasing batch size; this is unlike GSM which was observed to have marginal gains beyond $B=2$ for Gaussian targets (Modi et al., 2023).
We also observe that the gradient-based methods (ADVI, Score, Fisher) have similar performance in terms of convergence, and the score-based divergence is typically more sensitive to the learning rate. In Appendix E.2, we present wallclock timings for the methods, which show that the gradient evaluations dominate the computational cost in lower-dimensional settings.

Non-Gaussian targets with varying skew and tails. The sinh-arcsinh normal distribution transforms a Gaussian random variable via the hyperbolic sine function and its inverse (Jones \& Pewsey, 2009; 2019). If $y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$, then a sample from the sinh-arcsinh normal distribution is
\[
z=\sinh \left(\frac{1}{\tau}\left(\sinh ^{-1}(y)+s\right)\right)
\]
where the parameters $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\tau>0$ control, respectively, the skew and the heaviness of the tails. The Gaussian distribution is recovered when $s=0$ and $\tau=1$.
We construct different non-Gaussian target distributions by varying these parameters. The results are presented in Figure 5.2 and Figure E.4. Here we use a decaying learning rate $\lambda_{t}=B D /(t+1)$ for BaM , as some decay is necessary for BaM to converge when the target distribution is nonGaussian.

First, we construct target distributions with normal tails ( $t=1$ ) but varying skew ( $s=0.2,1.0,1.8$ ). Here we observe that BaM converges faster than ADVI. For large skew ( $s=1.0,1.8$ ), BaM converges to a higher value of the forward KL divergence but to similar values of the reverse KL divergence. In these experiments, we see that GSM and ADVI often have similar performance but that BaM stabilizes more quickly with larger batch sizes. Notably, the reverse KL divergence for GSM diverges when the target distribution is highly skewed ( $s=1.8$ ). The Score method diverges for highly skewed targets as well, and we found this method to be more sensitive to the learning rate.

Next we construct target distributions with no skew ( $s=0$ ) but tails of varying heaviness $(t=0.1,0.9,1.7)$. Here we find that all methods tend to converge to similar values of the reverse KL divergence. In some cases, BaM and ADVI converge to better values than GSM, and BaM typically converges in fewer gradient evaluations than ADVI.

\subsection*{5.2. Application: hierarchical Bayesian models}

We now consider the application of BaM to posterior inference. Suppose we have observations $\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}$, and the target distribution is the posterior density
\[
p\left(z \mid\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}\right) \propto p(z) p\left(\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N} \mid z\right)
\]
with prior $p(z)$ and likelihood $p\left(\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N} \mid z\right)$. We examine three target distributions from posteriordb (Magnusson et al., 2022), a database of Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017; Roualdes et al., 2023) models with reference samples generated using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). The first target is nearly Gaussian (ark, D=7). The other

two targets are non-Gaussian: one is a Gaussian process (GP) Poisson regression model (gp-pois-regr, $D=13$ ), and the other is the 8 -schools hierarchical Bayesian model (eight-schools-centered, $D=10$ ).

In these experiments, we evaluate $\mathrm{BaM}, \mathrm{ADVI}$, and GSM by computing the relative errors of the posterior mean and standard deviation (SD) estimates with respect to those from HMC samples (Welandawe et al., 2022); we define these quantities and present additional results in Appendix E.5. We use a decaying learning rate $\lambda_{t}=B D /(t+1)$ for BaM.
Figure 5.3 compares the relative mean errors of BaM , ADVI, and GSM for batch sizes $B=8$ and $B=32$. We observe that BaM outperforms ADVI. For smaller batch sizes GSM can converge faster than BaM , but it oscillates around the solution. \subsection*{5.3. Application: deep generative model}

In a deep generative model, the likelihood is parameterized by the output of a neural network $\Omega$, e.g.,
\[
\begin{aligned}
z_{n} & \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \\
x_{n} \mid z_{n} & \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\Omega\left(z_{n}, \hat{\theta}\right), \sigma^{2} I\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where $x_{n}$ corresponds to a high-dimensional object, such as an image, and $z_{n}$ is a low-dimensional representation of $x_{n}$. The neural network $\Omega$ is parameterized by $\hat{\theta}$ and maps $z_{n}$ to the mean of the likelihood $p\left(x_{n} \mid z_{n}\right)$. For this example, we set $\sigma^{2}=0.1$. The above joint distribution underlies many deep learning models (Tomczak, 2022), including the variational autoencoder (Kingma \& Welling, 2014; Rezende et al., 2014). We train the neural network on the CIFAR-10 image data set (Krizhevsky, 2009). We model the images as continuous, with $x_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{3072}$, and learn a latent representation $z_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$; see Appendix E. 6 for details.

Given a new observation $x^{\prime}$, we wish to approximate the posterior $p\left(z^{\prime} \mid x^{\prime}\right)$. As an evaluation metric, we examine
how well $x^{\prime}$ is reconstructed by feeding the posterior expectation $\mathbb{E}\left[z^{\prime} \mid x^{\prime}\right]$ into the neural network $\Omega(\cdot, \hat{\theta})$. The quality of the reconstruction is assessed visually and using the mean squared error (MSE, Figure 5.4); we present the MSE plotted against wallclock time in Figure E.7. For ADVI and BaM , we use a pilot run of $T=100$ iterations to find a suitable learning rate; we then run the algorithms for $T=1000$ iterations. (GSM does not require this tuning step.) BaM performs poorly when the batch size is very small $(B=10)$ relative to the dimension of the latent variable $z^{\prime}$, but it becomes competitive as the batch size is increased. When the batch size is comparable to the dimension of $z_{n}$ (i.e. $B=300$ ), BaM converges an order of magnitude (or more) faster than ADVI and GSM.

To refine our comparison, suppose we have a computational budget of 3000 gradient evaluations. Under this budget, ADVI achieves its lowest MSE for $B=10$ and $T=300$, while BaM produces a comparable result for $B=300$ and $T=10$. Hence, the gradient evaluations for BaM can be largely parallelized. By contrast, most gradients for ADVI must be evaluated sequentially. Notably, Figure E. 7 shows that BaM with $B=300$ converges faster in wallclock time.
Depending on how the parameter $\hat{\theta}$ of the neural network is estimated, it possible to learn an encoder and perform amortized variational inference (AVI) on a new observation $x^{\prime}$. When such an encoder is available, estimations of $p\left(z^{\prime} \mid x^{\prime}\right)$ can be obtained essentially for free. In our experiment, both BaM and ADVI eventually achieve a lower reconstruction error than AVI. This result is expected because our AVI implementation uses a factorized Gaussian approximation, whereas BaM and ADVI use a full-covariance approximation, and the latter provides better compression of $x^{\prime}$ even though the dimension of $z^{\prime}$ and the weights of the neural network remain unchanged.

"""BaM, GSM and gradient-based BBVI (ADVI / Score / Fisher) for full-covariance Gaussians, in JAX.

All algorithms take `logp` (unnormalised log target, R^D -> R) and return traces of (mu, Sigma)
at recorded iterations. The cost axis is #gradient evaluations = iteration * B.
"""
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)


def _sym_sqrt(M):
    w, Q = jnp.linalg.eigh(0.5 * (M + M.T))
    return (Q * jnp.sqrt(jnp.clip(w, 0.0))) @ Q.T


def bam_update(mu, Sigma, z, g, lam):
    """One BaM match step (Algorithm 1), given batch samples z (B,D) and scores g (B,D)."""
    D = mu.shape[0]
    zbar = z.mean(0)
    gbar = g.mean(0)
    zc = z - zbar
    gc = g - gbar
    C = zc.T @ zc / z.shape[0]
    Gamma = gc.T @ gc / z.shape[0]
    U = lam * Gamma + lam / (1 + lam) * jnp.outer(gbar, gbar)
    dm = mu - zbar
    V = Sigma + lam * C + lam / (1 + lam) * jnp.outer(dm, dm)
    # Symmetric form of Sigma = 2V (I + (I+4UV)^{1/2})^{-1}:
    #   Sigma = V^{1/2} 2 (I + (I + 4 V^{1/2} U V^{1/2})^{1/2})^{-1} V^{1/2}
    Vh = _sym_sqrt(V)
    W = _sym_sqrt(jnp.eye(D) + 4 * Vh @ U @ Vh)
    w, Q = jnp.linalg.eigh(0.5 * (W + W.T))
    inner = (Q * (2.0 / (1.0 + w))) @ Q.T
    Snew = Vh @ inner @ Vh
    Snew = 0.5 * (Snew + Snew.T)
    munew = mu / (1 + lam) + lam / (1 + lam) * (Snew @ gbar + zbar)
    return munew, Snew


def gsm_update(mu, Sigma, z, g):
    """GSM batch update (Algorithm 3, Modi et al. 2023)."""
    def one(zb, sb):
        eps = Sigma @ sb - mu + zb
        dmz = mu - zb
        c = sb @ Sigma @ sb + (dmz @ sb) ** 2
        rho = 0.5 * (-1 + jnp.sqrt(1 + 4 * c))
        denom = 1 + rho + dmz @ sb
        dmu = (eps - dmz * (sb @ eps) / denom) / (1 + rho)
        mut = mu + dmu
        dS = jnp.outer(dmz, dmz) - jnp.outer(mut - zb, mut - zb)
        return dmu, dS
    dmu, dS = jax.vmap(one)(z, g)
    return mu + dmu.mean(0), Sigma + dS.mean(0)


def _chol_or_jitter(S):
    D = S.shape[0]
    S = 0.5 * (S + S.T)
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(S)
    L2 = jnp.linalg.cholesky(S + 1e-8 * jnp.trace(S) / D * jnp.eye(D))
    return jnp.where(jnp.any(jnp.isnan(L)), L2, L)


def run_bam_or_gsm(logp, D, B, T, key, mu0, S0, method="bam", lam_fn=None, record_every=1):
    """Run BaM or GSM for T iterations; returns stacked (mu, Sigma) every `record_every` iters
    (including the initial point). lam_fn(t) gives lambda_t for BaM."""
    score = jax.vmap(jax.grad(logp))

    def step(carry, t):
        mu, S, key = carry
        key, sk = jax.random.split(key)
        L = _chol_or_jitter(S)
        z = mu + jax.random.normal(sk, (B, D)) @ L.T
        g = score(z)
        if method == "bam":
            mun, Sn = bam_update(mu, S, z, g, lam_fn(t))
        else:
            mun, Sn = gsm_update(mu, S, z, g)
        bad = jnp.any(~jnp.isfinite(mun)) | jnp.any(~jnp.isfinite(Sn))
        # keep NaNs out of the state (record divergence as-is would poison everything)
        mun = jnp.where(bad, mu, mun)
        Sn = jnp.where(bad, S, Sn)
        return (mun, Sn, key), None

    def outer(carry, t0):
        carry, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, carry, t0 * record_every + jnp.arange(record_every))
        return carry, (carry[0], carry[1])

    n_rec = T // record_every
    (_, _, _), (mus, Ss) = jax.jit(lambda c: jax.lax.scan(outer, c, jnp.arange(n_rec)))((mu0, S0, key))
    mus = jnp.concatenate([mu0[None], mus])
    Ss = jnp.concatenate([S0[None], Ss])
    iters = jnp.arange(n_rec + 1) * record_every
    return iters * B, mus, Ss


def run_gradient_vi(logp, D, B, T, key, mu0, S0, loss="elbo", lr=1e-2, record_every=1):
    """ADVI-style optimisation with Adam over (mu, L) where Sigma = L L^T, L lower-triangular
    with positive (exp-parameterised) diagonal.  loss in {'elbo', 'score', 'fisher'}."""
    grad_logp = jax.grad(logp)
    L0 = jnp.linalg.cholesky(S0)
    params0 = {"mu": mu0, "Loff": jnp.tril(L0, -1), "logd": jnp.log(jnp.diag(L0))}
    tril_mask = jnp.tril(jnp.ones((D, D)), -1)

    def getL(p):
        return p["Loff"] * tril_mask + jnp.diag(jnp.exp(p["logd"]))

    def lossfn(p, eps):
        L = getL(p)
        z = p["mu"] + eps @ L.T
        if loss == "elbo":
            # -ELBO up to const: -E[log p] - entropy
            return -jnp.mean(jax.vmap(logp)(z)) - jnp.sum(p["logd"])
        gp = jax.vmap(grad_logp)(z)
        # grad log q(z) = -Sigma^{-1}(z-mu) = -L^{-T} eps
        gq = -jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(L.T, eps.T, lower=False).T
        diff = gq - gp
        if loss == "score":
            Sigma = L @ L.T
            return jnp.mean(jnp.sum((diff @ Sigma) * diff, -1))
        return jnp.mean(jnp.sum(diff * diff, -1))

    opt = optax.adam(lr)
    state0 = opt.init(params0)

    def step(carry, _):
        p, s, key = carry
        key, sk = jax.random.split(key)
        eps = jax.random.normal(sk, (B, D))
        gr = jax.grad(lossfn)(p, eps)
        upd, s = opt.update(gr, s, p)
        pn = optax.apply_updates(p, upd)
        ok = jnp.all(jnp.array([jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(v)) for v in jax.tree_util.tree_leaves(pn)]))
        pn = jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda a, b: jnp.where(ok, a, b), pn, p)
        return (pn, s, key), None

    def outer(carry, _):
        carry, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=record_every)
        L = getL(carry[0])
        return carry, (carry[0]["mu"], L @ L.T)

    n_rec = T // record_every
    _, (mus, Ss) = jax.jit(lambda c: jax.lax.scan(outer, c, None, length=n_rec))((params0, state0, key))
    mus = jnp.concatenate([mu0[None], mus])
    Ss = jnp.concatenate([S0[None], Ss])
    iters = jnp.arange(n_rec + 1) * record_every
    return iters * B, mus, Ss


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- metrics
def gauss_kl(m0, S0, m1, S1):
    """KL(N(m0,S0) || N(m1,S1))."""
    D = m0.shape[0]
    L1 = jnp.linalg.cholesky(S1)
    L0 = jnp.linalg.cholesky(S0)
    A = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(L1, L0, lower=True)
    d = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(L1, m1 - m0, lower=True)
    return 0.5 * (jnp.sum(A * A) + d @ d - D) + jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(L1))) - jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(L0)))


def gauss_logpdf(z, m, S):
    D = m.shape[0]
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(S)
    r = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(L, (z - m).T, lower=True)
    return -0.5 * jnp.sum(r * r, 0) - jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(L))) - 0.5 * D * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi)

import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from algorithms import run_bam_or_gsm, run_gradient_vi, gauss_kl

p.add_argument("--dims", type=int, nargs="+", default=[4, 16, 64, 256])
p.add_argument("--budget", type=int, default=20000, help="# gradient evaluations")
p.add_argument("--seeds", type=int, default=10)

LRS = [1e-3, 5e-3, 1e-2, 2e-2, 5e-2]
NREC = 200


def make_target(D, seed=1234):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed + D)
    A = rng.normal(size=(D, D))
    S = A @ A.T + 1e-3 * np.eye(D)
    m = rng.normal(size=D)
    return jnp.array(m), jnp.array(S)


def kls(mt, St, mus, Ss):
    def f(m, S):
        ok = jnp.all(jnp.linalg.eigvalsh(0.5 * (S + S.T)) > 0)
        Sp = jnp.where(ok, S, jnp.eye(m.shape[0]))
        fk = gauss_kl(mt, St, m, Sp)
        rk = gauss_kl(m, Sp, mt, St)
        return jnp.where(ok, fk, jnp.nan), jnp.where(ok, rk, jnp.nan)
    fk, rk = jax.jit(jax.vmap(f))(mus, Ss)
    return np.asarray(fk), np.asarray(rk)


def run(method, D, B, seed, mt, St, lr=None):
    logp = lambda z: -0.5 * (z - mt) @ jnp.linalg.solve(St, z - mt)
    Sinv = jnp.linalg.inv(St)
    logp = lambda z: -0.5 * (z - mt) @ Sinv @ (z - mt)
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed)
    k0, key = jax.random.split(key)
    mu0 = jax.random.uniform(k0, (D,), minval=0.0, maxval=0.1)
    S0 = jnp.eye(D)
    T = a.budget // B
    rec = max(1, T // NREC)
    T = rec * (T // rec)

    def load(fn):

            b = pickle.load(f, encoding="bytes")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------- model
class Encoder(nn.Module):
    c: int
    @nn.compact
    def __call__(self, x):
        c = self.c
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(c, (3, 3), strides=2)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(c, (3, 3), strides=1)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=2)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=1)(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=2)(x))
        x = x.reshape(x.shape[0], -1)
        mu = nn.Dense(LATENT)(x)
        logvar = nn.Dense(LATENT)(x)       # factorized Gaussian encoder
        return mu, logvar


class Decoder(nn.Module):
    c: int
    @nn.compact
    def __call__(self, z):
        c = self.c
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Dense(4 * 4 * 2 * c)(z)).reshape(z.shape[0], 4, 4, 2 * c)
        x = nn.gelu(nn.ConvTranspose(2 * c, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(2 * c, (3, 3))(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.ConvTranspose(c, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x))
        x = nn.gelu(nn.Conv(c, (3, 3))(x))
        x = nn.ConvTranspose(3, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x)
        return jnp.tanh(x)

        xh = dec.apply(p["dec"], z)
        ll = -0.5 * jnp.sum((x - xh) ** 2, axis=(1, 2, 3)) / SIG2
        kl = 0.5 * jnp.sum(jnp.exp(lv) + mu ** 2 - 1.0 - lv, axis=1)
        return jnp.mean(kl - ll)

    def step(p, s, x, key):
        l, g = jax.value_and_grad(negelbo)(p, x, key)
        u, s = opt.update(g, s, p)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------- BBVI
def make_target(dec, dparams, xp):
    xp = jnp.asarray(xp, jnp.float32)

    def logp(z):  # z: (D,) float64
        z32 = z.astype(jnp.float32)
        xh = dec.apply(dparams, z32[None])[0]
        return (-0.5 * jnp.sum(z32 ** 2) - 0.5 * jnp.sum((xp - xh) ** 2) / SIG2).astype(jnp.float64)

    score = jax.jit(jax.vmap(jax.grad(logp)))
    vlogp_grad = jax.vmap(jax.grad(logp))

    @jax.jit
    def mse(mu):
        xh = dec.apply(dparams, mu.astype(jnp.float32)[None])[0]
        return jnp.mean((xp - xh) ** 2)
    return logp, score, vlogp_grad, mse


def sqrtm_psd(A):
    w, U = jnp.linalg.eigh(0.5 * (A + A.T))
    return (U * jnp.sqrt(jnp.clip(w, 0.0))) @ U.T


def make_bam_step(vgrad, D, B):
    @jax.jit
    def step(mu, Sig, lam, key):
        L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Sig + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(D))
        z = mu + jax.random.normal(key, (B, D)) @ L.T
        g = vgrad(z)
        zb, gb = z.mean(0), g.mean(0)
        C = (z - zb).T @ (z - zb) / B
        G = (g - gb).T @ (g - gb) / B
        U = lam * G + lam / (1 + lam) * jnp.outer(gb, gb)
        dm = mu - zb
        V = Sig + lam * C + lam / (1 + lam) * jnp.outer(dm, dm)
        Vh = sqrtm_psd(V)
        M = jnp.eye(D) + sqrtm_psd(jnp.eye(D) + 4 * Vh @ U @ Vh)
        Snew = 2.0 * Vh @ jnp.linalg.solve(M, Vh)
        Snew = 0.5 * (Snew + Snew.T)
        mnew = mu / (1 + lam) + lam / (1 + lam) * (Snew @ gb + zb)
        return mnew, Snew
    return step


def make_gsm_step(vgrad, D, B):
    @jax.jit
    def step(mu, Sig, key):
        L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Sig + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(D))
        z = mu + jax.random.normal(key, (B, D)) @ L.T
        s = vgrad(z)

        def one(zb, sb):
            Ss = Sig @ sb
            eps = Ss - mu + zb
            d = mu - zb
            ds = d @ sb
            c = sb @ Ss + ds ** 2
            rho = 0.5 * (-1.0 + jnp.sqrt(1.0 + 4.0 * c))
            dmu = (eps - d * (sb @ eps) / (1 + rho + ds)) / (1 + rho)
            mt = mu + dmu
            dS = jnp.outer(d, d) - jnp.outer(mt - zb, mt - zb)
            return dmu, dS
        dmu, dS = jax.vmap(one)(z, s)
        Snew = Sig + dS.mean(0)
        return mu + dmu.mean(0), 0.5 * (Snew + Snew.T)
    return step


def make_advi(vgrad_unused, logp, D, B, lr):
    opt = optax.adam(lr)
    vlogp = jax.vmap(logp)
    tril = jnp.tril_indices(D, -1)

    def unpack(p):
        L = jnp.zeros((D, D)).at[tril].set(p["off"]) + jnp.diag(jnp.exp(p["logd"]))
        return L

    def loss(p, key):
        L = unpack(p)
        z = p["mu"] + jax.random.normal(key, (B, D)) @ L.T
        return -(jnp.mean(vlogp(z)) + jnp.sum(p["logd"]))   # negative ELBO (up to const)

    @jax.jit
    def step(p, s, key):
        g = jax.grad(loss)(p, key)
        u, s = opt.update(g, s, p)
        return optax.apply_updates(p, u), s

    p0 = {"mu": jnp.zeros(D), "off": jnp.zeros(len(tril[0])), "logd": jnp.zeros(D)}
    return step, opt.init(p0), p0


def record_iters(T, B):
    its = set(range(0, min(T, 50) + 1))
    its |= set(range(0, T + 1, 5 if B >= 100 else 10))
    its.add(T)
    return its


def run(method, B, T, hp, ctx, seed=1):
    D = LATENT
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed)
    mse = ctx["mse"]
    rec = record_iters(T, B)
    evals, errs = [], []
    if method in ("bam", "gsm"):
        mu, Sig = jnp.zeros(D), jnp.eye(D)
        step = ctx[(method, B)]
        for t in range(T + 1):
            if t in rec:
                e = float(mse(mu))
                evals.append(t * B); errs.append(e if np.isfinite(e) else np.nan)
                if not np.isfinite(e):
                    break
            if t == T:
                break
            key, k = jax.random.split(key)
            mu, Sig = step(mu, Sig, hp, k) if method == "bam" else step(mu, Sig, k)
    else:
        step, s, p = make_advi(None, ctx["logp"], D, B, hp)
        for t in range(T + 1):
            if t in rec:
                e = float(mse(p["mu"]))
                evals.append(t * B); errs.append(e if np.isfinite(e) else np.nan)
                if not np.isfinite(e):

            if t == T:

            key, k = jax.random.split(key)
            p, s = step(p, s, k)

def pick(results):
    """lowest final pilot MSE; near-ties (within 2%) broken by mean MSE over the pilot (speed)."""
    fin = {h: (r[1][-1] if len(r[1]) and np.isfinite(r[1][-1]) and len(r[0]) and r[0][-1] == r[0][-1] else np.inf)

"""Section 5.2: hierarchical Bayesian models from posteriordb (Figure 5.3 / E.6).

Models are re-implemented in JAX on Stan's unconstrained space (log for positive params, incl. Jacobian),
instead of via bridgestan (no Stan toolchain needed). Reference posterior mean/SD (unconstrained space)
come from the posteriordb HMC reference draws (vendored in pdb_data/).
"""
import argparse, json, os, time, zipfile
import numpy as np
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.scipy.stats import norm, gamma, cauchy
from algorithms import run_bam_or_gsm, run_gradient_vi

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--budget", type=int, default=10000)
p.add_argument("--seeds", type=int, default=5)
p.add_argument("--out", default="results/pdb")
a = p.parse_args()
os.makedirs(a.out, exist_ok=True)
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
LRS = [1e-3, 5e-3, 1e-2, 2e-2, 5e-2, 1e-1]
NREC = 100


def load(name):
    return json.load(open(os.path.join(HERE, "pdb_data", name + ".json")))


def load_draws(name):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(os.path.join(HERE, "pdb_data", name + ".json.zip")) as z:
        d = json.loads(z.read(z.namelist()[0]))
    return {k: np.concatenate([np.asarray(c[k]) for c in d]) for k in d[0]}


# ---------------- arK (D=7): z = (alpha, beta[1:5], log sigma)
def ark():
    dat = load("arK"); K, T = dat["K"], dat["T"]; y = jnp.array(dat["y"])
    X = jnp.stack([y[K - k - 1:T - k - 1] for k in range(K)], 1)  # y[t-k], k=1..K
    yt = y[K:]
    def logp(z):
        al, be, ls = z[0], z[1:1 + K], z[-1]
        sig = jnp.exp(ls)
        lp = norm.logpdf(al, 0, 10) + norm.logpdf(be, 0, 10).sum() + cauchy.logpdf(sig, 0, 2.5) + ls
        return lp + norm.logpdf(yt, al + X @ be, sig).sum()
    dr = load_draws("arK-arK")
    ref = np.stack([dr["alpha"]] + [dr[f"beta[{k}]"] for k in range(1, K + 1)] + [np.log(dr["sigma"])], 1)
    return logp, ref


# ---------------- gp_pois_regr (D=13): z = (log rho, log alpha, f_tilde[1:11])
def gp_cov(x, al, rho):
    d = x[:, None] - x[None, :]
    return al ** 2 * jnp.exp(-0.5 * d ** 2 / rho ** 2) + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(x.shape[0])


def gp():
    dat = load("gp_pois_regr"); x = jnp.array(dat["x"], dtype=float); k = jnp.array(dat["k"])
    def logp(z):
        lr, la, ft = z[0], z[1], z[2:]
        rho, al = jnp.exp(lr), jnp.exp(la)
        f = jnp.linalg.cholesky(gp_cov(x, al, rho)) @ ft
        lp = gamma.logpdf(rho, 25, scale=1 / 4.) + lr + norm.logpdf(al, 0, 2) + la + norm.logpdf(ft).sum()
        return lp + jnp.sum(k * f - jnp.exp(f))
    dr = load_draws("gp_pois_regr-gp_pois_regr")
    N = x.shape[0]
    F = np.stack([dr[f"f[{i}]"] for i in range(1, N + 1)], 1)
    Ls = jax.vmap(lambda a_, r_: jnp.linalg.cholesky(gp_cov(x, a_, r_)))(dr["alpha"], dr["rho"])
    ft = np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda L, f: jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(L, f, lower=True))(Ls, F))
    ref = np.concatenate([np.log(dr["rho"])[:, None], np.log(dr["alpha"])[:, None], ft], 1)
    return logp, ref


# ---------------- eight_schools_centered (D=10): z = (theta[1:8], mu, log tau)
def eight():
    dat = load("eight_schools"); y = jnp.array(dat["y"], dtype=float); s = jnp.array(dat["sigma"], dtype=float)
    def logp(z):
        th, mu, lt = z[:8], z[8], z[9]
        tau = jnp.exp(lt)
        lp = cauchy.logpdf(tau, 0, 5) + lt + norm.logpdf(th, mu, tau).sum() + norm.logpdf(mu, 0, 5)
        return lp + norm.logpdf(y, th, s).sum()
    # same posterior over (theta, mu, tau) as the non-centered reference (theta is a generated quantity there)
    dr = load_draws("eight_schools-eight_schools_noncentered")
    ref = np.stack([dr[f"theta[{i}]"] for i in range(1, 9)] + [dr["mu"], np.log(dr["tau"])], 1)
    return logp, ref


def errors(mus, Ss, rm, rs):
    sd = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.diagonal(Ss, axis1=-2, axis2=-1), 0, None))
    me = np.linalg.norm((rm - mus) / rs, axis=-1)
    se = np.linalg.norm((rs - sd) / rs, axis=-1)
    return me, se


for name, fn in [("ark", ark), ("gp_pois_regr", gp), ("eight_schools_centered", eight)]:
    logp, ref = fn()
    D = ref.shape[1]
    rm, rs = ref.mean(0), ref.std(0)
    t0 = time.time()

    def run(method, B, seeds, lr=None):
        ks = jnp.stack([jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(sd), 2) for sd in seeds])
        mu0 = jax.vmap(lambda k: jax.random.uniform(k, (D,), minval=0.0, maxval=0.1))(ks[:, 0])
        S0 = jnp.eye(D)
        T = a.budget // B
        rec = max(1, T // NREC)
        T = rec * (T // rec)
        if method == "bam":
            ge, mus, Ss = run_bam_or_gsm(logp, D, B, T, ks[:, 1], mu0, S0, "bam", lambda t: B * D / (t + 1.0), rec)
        elif method == "gsm":
            ge, mus, Ss = run_bam_or_gsm(logp, D, B, T, ks[:, 1], mu0, S0, "gsm", None, rec)
        else:
            ge, mus, Ss = run_gradient_vi(logp, D, B, T, ks[:, 1], mu0, S0, "elbo", lr, rec)
        me, se = errors(np.asarray(mus), np.asarray(Ss), rm, rs)
        return np.asarray(ge), me, se

    res = {}
    for B in [8, 32]:
        # ADVI learning-rate grid search (2 pilot seeds, criterion: final relative mean error)
        sc = {}
        for lr in LRS:
            _, me, _ = run("elbo", B, [100, 101], lr)
            tail = me[:, -me.shape[1] // 10:]
            sc[lr] = float(np.mean(tail)) if np.isfinite(tail).all() else np.inf
        blr = min(sc, key=lambda k: sc[k])
        print(f"{name} ADVI B={B} grid {sc} -> {blr}", flush=True)
        for m in ["bam", "gsm", "elbo"]:
            ge, me, se = run(m, B, list(range(a.seeds)), blr if m == "elbo" else None)
            lab = {"bam": "BaM", "gsm": "GSM", "elbo": "ADVI"}[m] + f"-{B}"
            res[lab] = dict(ge=ge.tolist(), mean_err=me.tolist(), sd_err=se.tolist(), lr=blr if m == "elbo" else None)
            print(f"{name} {lab}: final rel mean err {np.nanmean(me[:, -1]):.3g}  rel SD err {np.nanmean(se[:, -1]):.3g} ({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)", flush=True)
    with open(f"{a.out}/pdb_{name}.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(res, f)

"""Make figures from results/*.json (whatever exists)."""
import glob, json, os, sys
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

R = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "results"
COL = {"ADVI": "#e9a36b", "Score": "#d9542c", "Fisher": "#f08c5a", "GSM": "#c2185b"}


def col(name):
    for k, v in COL.items():
        if name.startswith(k):
            return v
    return "#3b0f40" if name.startswith("BaM") and not name.endswith("-2") and not name.endswith("-5") else "#7b2d6e"


def panel(ax, res, key, title, logx=True):
    for name, r in res.items():
        y = np.array(r[key], dtype=float)
        x = np.array(r["ge"], dtype=float)
        x = np.maximum(x, 1)
        y = np.clip(y, 1e-8, None)
        m = np.nanmean(y, 0)
        ax.plot(x, m, label=name, color=col(name), lw=1.8,
                ls="--" if name.endswith("-8") else "-")
        for row in y:
            ax.plot(x, row, color=col(name), alpha=0.12, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    if logx:
        ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("# gradient evaluations")


for key, lab in [("fwd", "Forward KL"), ("rev", "Reverse KL")]:
    files = sorted(glob.glob(f"{R}/gaussian/gaussian_D*.json"), key=lambda f: int(f.split("_D")[1][:-5]))
    if files:
        fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(files), figsize=(4 * len(files), 3.2), squeeze=False)
        for ax, f in zip(axs[0], files):
            panel(ax, json.load(open(f)), key, "D=" + f.split("_D")[1][:-5])
        axs[0, 0].set_ylabel(lab); axs[0, 0].legend(fontsize=7)
        fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(f"{R}/fig_gaussian_{key}.png", dpi=120); plt.close(fig)
    files = sorted(glob.glob(f"{R}/sinh/sinh_*.json"))
    if files:
        fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(files), figsize=(3.6 * len(files), 3.2), squeeze=False)
        for ax, f in zip(axs[0], files):
            b = os.path.basename(f)[5:-5]
            panel(ax, json.load(open(f)), key, b.replace("_t", ", tau=").replace("s", "s=", 1))
        axs[0, 0].set_ylabel(lab); axs[0, 0].legend(fontsize=7)
        fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(f"{R}/fig_sinh_{key}.png", dpi=120); plt.close(fig)

for key, lab in [("mean_err", "relative mean error"), ("sd_err", "relative SD error")]:
    files = sorted(glob.glob(f"{R}/pdb/pdb_*.json"))
    if files:
        fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(files), figsize=(4 * len(files), 3.2), squeeze=False)
        for ax, f in zip(axs[0], files):
            panel(ax, json.load(open(f)), key, os.path.basename(f)[4:-5])
        axs[0, 0].set_ylabel(lab); axs[0, 0].legend(fontsize=7)
        fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(f"{R}/fig_pdb_{key}.png", dpi=120); plt.close(fig)

# summary table
lines = []
for f in sorted(glob.glob(f"{R}/*/*.json")):
    res = json.load(open(f))
    for name, r in res.items():
        if not isinstance(r, dict) or "ge" not in r:
            continue
        ks = [k for k in ["fwd", "rev", "mean_err", "sd_err"] if k in r]
        vals = " ".join(f"{k}={np.nanmean(np.array(r[k], dtype=float)[:, -1]):.3g}" for k in ks)
        lines.append(f"{os.path.basename(f)[:-5]:40s} {name:10s} lr={r.get('lr')} final(mean over seeds): {vals}")
open(f"{R}/summary.txt", "w").write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
print("\n".join(lines))

# Reproduction: Batch and Match (BaM) — BBVI with a score-based divergence

This repo re-implements, from the paper alone, BaM (Algorithm 1) and the baselines
(ADVI, ADVI with score-based / Fisher divergence losses, GSM), all in JAX (float64, CPU), and runs
CPU-scaled versions of the main-text experiments.

## Layout
| file | content |
|---|---|
| `bam/algorithms.py` | BaM update (closed-form match step, symmetric form of eq. 12: `Σ = V^{1/2}·2(I+(I+4V^{1/2}UV^{1/2})^{1/2})^{-1}V^{1/2}`, mean update eq. 13), GSM (Alg. 3), gradient-based VI with Adam (Alg. 2; loss = negative ELBO, score-based divergence, or Fisher divergence; Σ=LLᵀ), Gaussian KL. All runs are `lax.scan`-compiled and `vmap`-ed over seeds. |
| `bam/exp_gaussian.py` | Sec 5.1, Gaussian targets D=4,16,64,256 (Fig 5.1 / E.3): forward and reverse KL vs #gradient evaluations. BaM with λ=BD and B∈{2, B_large}; others B=2; learning-rate grid search {1e-3,5e-3,1e-2,2e-2,5e-2} for ADVI/Score/Fisher. |
| `bam/exp_sinh.py` | Sec 5.1, sinh-arcsinh targets D=10 (skew s∈{0.2,1,1.8}, τ=1; s=0, τ∈{0.1,0.9,1.7}) (Fig 5.2 / E.4). BaM λ_t=BD/(t+1), B∈{5,10}; others B=5; lr grid search. Forward KL is estimated with exact samples from p, reverse KL with samples from q. |
| `bam/exp_pdb.py` | Sec 5.2, posteriordb models ark (D=7), gp_pois_regr (D=13), eight_schools_centered (D=10) (Fig 5.3 / E.6): relative mean and SD errors vs HMC reference draws, B∈{8,32}, BaM λ_t=BD/(t+1), ADVI lr grid search. |
| `bam/pdb_data/` | data + reference HMC draws downloaded from the public posteriordb repository. |
| `bam/plot.py` | figures `results/fig_*.png` and `results/summary.txt`. |
| `vae/` | Sec 5.3 deep generative model (CIFAR-10 VAE + posterior inference over z'∈R^256), reduced budget; see `vae/README_vae.md`. |
| `reproduce.sh` | runs everything (`QUICK=1 bash reproduce.sh` for a smoke run). |

## Deviations from the paper (honest list)
* **No bridgestan/Stan**: the three posteriordb models are hand-written in JAX on Stan's unconstrained
  space (log-transform for positive parameters + Jacobian). Errors are measured in this unconstrained space.
  For eight_schools_centered the reference draws are those of the non-centered posterior (same posterior over θ, μ, τ).
* **Compute**: everything had to run on a shared 8-core CPU within a 90 min session. Budgets: 2·10⁴ gradient
  evaluations for Gaussian D≤64 and sinh-arcsinh (paper ≈4·10⁴); D=256 used 10⁴ evaluations, 3 seeds and the
  learning rates the paper reports (ADVI 0.01, Score 0.001, Fisher 0.01) instead of a grid search;
  sinh heavy-tail targets used 5 seeds and 1 grid seed; posteriordb used 5·10³ evaluations, 5 seeds.
* Target construction details not in the paper were chosen by us: Gaussian targets Σ*=AAᵀ (A iid N(0,1)) with random
  N(0,1) mean; sinh-arcsinh base Gaussian Σ=AAᵀ/D+0.1I, random mean.
* Learning-rate selection criterion: final forward KL (Gaussian), final reverse KL (sinh-arcsinh; forward KL
  estimates are very noisy for heavy tails), final relative mean error (posteriordb).

See `RESULTS.md` for what was actually obtained.

# Section 5.3 (deep generative model / VAE) -- reduced-budget reproduction

Run from `/home/submission`: `python vae/run_vae.py` (deps in `vae/requirements.txt`; JAX + flax + optax, CPU).
Log of the reported run: `vae/run_log.txt`; outputs: `vae/results/vae_results.json`, `vae/results/vae_mse.png`
(json and figure are rewritten after each batch size finishes, so partial runs still leave usable output).

## What the script does
1. Streams `cifar-10-python.tar.gz` into `vae/data/` (gitignored). It extracts `test_batch` plus the first
   `N_TRAIN_BATCHES` (default 1) training batches found in the archive (that is `data_batch_4`, 10k images), then
   stops downloading. Images are scaled to [-1, 1].
2. Trains a conv VAE with the addendum architecture: 5-conv encoder (stride 2/1/2/1/2), a dense layer to a
   factorized Gaussian (mean and log-variance heads), a dense + 3 ConvTranspose / 2 Conv decoder, GELU, tanh output,
   latent_dim = 256, Gaussian likelihood with sigma^2 = 0.1, 1-sample ELBO, and Adam with linear warmup (100 steps)
   followed by cosine decay to 1e-5.
3. Takes test image `x'` (index 0) with target `log p(z'|x') = log N(z';0,I) + log N(x'; dec(z'), 0.1 I)` and runs
   BaM (Alg. 1, symmetric sqrt form, float64 numpy eigh), ADVI (reparameterized ELBO, Adam, mean + Cholesky factor
   with log-diagonal), and GSM (Alg. 3). All three use full-covariance Gaussians initialized at N(0, I), with
   B = 10, 100, 300. BaM's lambda and ADVI's lr are picked by a pilot run from the grids in appendix E.6 by lowest
   final pilot MSE. Near-ties (within 2%) go to the setting with the lowest mean MSE over the pilot, i.e. the
   one that converged fastest.
   Metric: MSE(x', dec(mu_t)) vs. gradient evaluations t*B. The amortized-encoder (AVI) MSE is the dashed line.

## Reductions vs. the paper (forced by the time limit and a heavily shared CPU)
The machine was shared with other jobs (load average about 20 on 8 cores), so XLA compiles took 1-2 minutes each.
- VAE: c_hid = 16, trained on 10k images (one CIFAR batch) for about 5 epochs (200 s wall-clock cap) instead of
  the full set for 100 epochs. The peak lr was raised from 1e-4 to 1e-3 to make up for the short training, and the
  cosine horizon is set for 30 epochs, so the lr barely decays. The decoder is therefore much weaker than the paper's.
- BBVI: T = 500 / 200 / 60 iterations for B = 10 / 100 / 300 (paper: 1000), and 50 pilot iterations (paper: 100).
  One test image and a single seed.

## Results
See `RESULTS` below (filled from `vae_results.json`).

Everything ran on a shared, oversubscribed 8-core CPU. The load average was about 17–20 because all experiments and the VAE run happened at once. Some runs were therefore unfinished when the session ended. Numbers come from `results/summary.txt` (the final value, averaged over seeds) and from the curves in `results/fig_*.png`. Rerun `bash reproduce.sh` to regenerate everything.

## Completed or partial runs

### 5.1 Gaussian targets (`results/fig_gaussian_{fwd,rev}.png`)
These used a budget of 2·10⁴ gradient evaluations and 10 seeds. Learning rates came from a grid search (2 seeds).

| D | BaM (B large, λ=BD) | BaM-2 | GSM-2 | ADVI-2 | Score-2 | Fisher-2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | ~1e-16 (exact) | ~1e-16 | ~1e-16 | 1.0e-2 | 4e-11 | 1.5e-4 |
| 16 | ~1e-16 | ~1e-16 | ~1e-16 | 1.6 | 72 | 92 |

The numbers are the final forward KL. The curves in the figure show BaM converging to machine precision within a few hundred gradient evaluations. A larger B makes it converge in fewer evaluations. GSM is competitive. ADVI, Score and Fisher are still far from converged at D=16 after 2·10⁴ evaluations, and Score was the most sensitive to the learning rate. This matches the paper's Fig. 5.1: BaM is orders of magnitude faster than ADVI.

**Not finished:** D=64 (only the ADVI and Score grid searches completed) and D=256 (no output at all), because of compute contention.

### 5.1 Sinh-arcsinh targets (D=10; `results/fig_sinh_{fwd,rev}.png`)
| target | BaM-10 fwd / rev | BaM-5 | GSM | ADVI | Score | Fisher |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s=0.2, τ=1 | 0.095 / 0.083 | 0.095 / 0.081 | 0.099 / 0.098 | 0.149 / 0.141 | 2.8e3 / 9.3 | 0.20 / 0.14 |
| s=1.0, τ=1 | 8.5 / 1.73 | 8.5 / 1.68 | 2.6 / **9.7** | 5.1 / 1.62 | 6.4e3 / 17 | 34 / 4.3 |
| s=0, τ=0.1 | 2e15 / 27 | 3e15 / 27 | diverged (NaN) | 5e13 / 22 | 6e17 / 39 | 2e15 / 30 |

Each cell gives forward / reverse KL. These trends agree with the paper:
- With small skew, BaM reaches the best value fastest.
- With large skew, BaM converges to a *higher forward KL* but a reverse KL similar to ADVI's.
- GSM's reverse KL is bad (9.7) under large skew.
- The Score method blows up on skewed targets.

At τ=0.1 the tails are extreme: z = sinh(10·asinh y). Every Gaussian therefore has an astronomically large forward KL estimate, the reverse KLs are similar across methods, and GSM went NaN.

**Not finished:** s=1.8, and τ=0.9 / 1.7. The τ=0.9 run had only completed BaM-10 (fwd 0.031, rev 0.020).

| ark rel. SD err | 4.0 | 0.02 | 3.9 | 0.04 | 0.02 | 7.0 |
| eight-schools rel. mean err | 0.34 | 0.35 | 3.25 | 0.38 | 0.34 | 2.7 |
| eight-schools rel. SD err | 1.07 | 0.79 | 1.67 | 1.10 | 0.94 | 1.58 |
| gp-pois-regr rel. mean err | diverged in 1/5 seeds | 0.70 | 15.3 | 2 of 5 seeds 0.33–0.42; 3 diverged | 38 (oscillates) | 15.1 |

These partly agree with the paper:
- BaM beats ADVI. BaM-32 is the most accurate on ark.
- BaM gets better with a larger batch, while GSM oscillates (gp, B=32).
- On eight-schools, BaM has a larger relative SD error than GSM, as the paper's Fig. E.6 notes.

Where it differs from the paper:
- With λ_0 = BD, the very first BaM step can jump to a region where the Poisson rate exp(f) overflows. Those gp runs then stay stuck. This happened in 1/5 seeds at B=8 and 3/5 at B=32, so the seed-averaged BaM error on gp is meaningless and should be read per seed.
- BaM-8 on ark is slow because of the 1/(t+1) learning-rate decay.

### 5.3 Deep generative model (`vae/`, see `vae/README_vae.md`)
This is a heavily reduced run: a weak VAE (c_hid=16, 10k training images, about 5 epochs) and shortened BBVI runs. Only B=10 finished. MSE on test image 0:

| method | MSE |
|---|---|
| BaM (λ=10) | 0.093 |
| ADVI (lr 0.05) | 0.117 |
| GSM | 0.125 |
| AVI encoder | 0.096 |

This does **not** match the paper's claim that BaM is poor at B=10, although the pilot selected λ=10 rather than the paper's 0.1. B=100 and B=300 did not finish, so the paper's main B=300 claim is untested here.

## Summary
- **Reproduced:** the core claims — BaM's closed-form updates converge orders of magnitude faster than ADVI-type methods on Gaussian targets, and BaM behaves as the paper describes on mildly non-Gaussian targets and on ark and eight-schools.
- **Not reproduced:** the high-dimensional Gaussian cases (D=64, 256), half of the sinh-arcsinh grid, and the B=100/300 VAE runs. All of these were missing for compute reasons only.
